A solver computes the field on a **mesh**: the model cut into small
tetrahedra. Every number it returns depends on that mesh. Refining the mesh
shows how much a number still moves, and a number you use should have stopped
moving by an amount that is small for your purpose. Refining changes only the
calculation, never the model: what is grounded, the box around the chip, the
route and the materials stay as you set them.

## What a mesh is {#mesh}

`mesh()` builds the model and fills every solution volume, the substrate and
the vacuum, with tetrahedra; a Route B conductor's inside gets none. On each
tetrahedron the solver approximates the field by a polynomial whose degree is
the FEM order (`set_numerical(order=...)`). The mesh recipe sets the starting
element sizes, and every tetrahedron must pass a shape-quality threshold:
SCGSim refines around those that do not, or stops with `MeshRepairError`.
The controls are in the
[Palace mesh reference](../reference/specs/palace-electrostatic-sgb.qmd#palace-mesh-controls).

## What refinement does {#refinement}

With adaptive refinement, Palace solves, estimates where its error is largest,
refines the mesh there and solves again. Each solve is one **pass**. In a
recorded study of the [First simulation](../start/first-simulation.qmd) pad
with a 10 nH junction ([run record](https://github.com/NCUPHY-LTLab/scgsim/issues/248#issuecomment-6873586635);
Palace Eigenmode, FEM order 2, Surface-EPR margins of 0.5 and 1 µm), four
passes gave:

| Pass | Tetrahedra | Mode 1 frequency | Change | MS participation, whole surface | Change | MS participation beyond 1 µm | Change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 117,138 | 5.122 GHz | | 1.033 × 10⁻⁴ | | 6.472 × 10⁻⁵ | |
| 2 | 179,515 | 5.132 GHz | +0.21 % | 1.075 × 10⁻⁴ | +4.1 % | 6.451 × 10⁻⁵ | −0.32 % |
| 3 | 517,335 | 5.139 GHz | +0.13 % | 1.211 × 10⁻⁴ | +13 % | 6.435 × 10⁻⁵ | −0.24 % |
| 4 | 1,445,206 | 5.143 GHz | +0.081 % | 1.348 × 10⁻⁴ | +11 % | 6.233 × 10⁻⁵ | −3.1 % |

Each change is from the pass before. Three quantities, three behaviours:

- **The frequency settles.** Each change is about 0.6 of the one before.
  Extrapolating those changes puts the limit at 5.1500 GHz, 0.13 % above
  pass 4.
- **The whole-surface participation does not settle.** It grows by 4 to 13 %
  at every pass. The growth is in the strip within 1 µm of the gap edges,
  whose share goes from 3.86 × 10⁻⁵ at pass 1 to 7.25 × 10⁻⁵ at pass 4 (the
  whole surface minus the part beyond 1 µm); that strip is what inset margins
  leave out ([Surface EPR](surface-epr.qmd#surface-distance-band-correction)).
- **The participation beyond 1 µm changes little, then jumps.** Two small
  changes in a row were followed by a 3.1 % one, so a single small change is
  not proof that a number has settled.

## Why convergence matters {#read-numerical-changes-beside-the-quantity}

Each quantity converges at its own rate, so judge the one you will use: a
frequency that has settled says nothing about a surface participation. To make
that judgement part of the run, **declare convergence**: name the numbers that
must stop changing and by how much. SCGSim then stops Palace at the first pass
where every criterion holds and reports which held and when.
[Convergence and reports](../guides/convergence-and-reports.qmd) shows how.

Palace's own indicators, its error estimate and the eigenvalue residual,
describe their own quantities, not your capacitance or participation. The
degree-of-freedom number in the mesh summary is an estimate of the problem's
size, not of its accuracy.

## What refinement does not change {#define-the-physical-model}

These choices define the model. Changing one gives a different model, not a
better-resolved one:

| Choice | Example |
|---|---|
| What is grounded | A box whose walls are grounded is a different model from one where only the chip's ground metal is at 0 V |
| The box around the chip | The vacuum region's size. Palace leaves its outer faces without a condition: for Eigenmode that is a perfect magnetic conductor (PMC), and HFSS assigns the same condition, Perfect H, on its Region. For Electrostatic, Palace assumes zero charge there |
| How the metal is drawn | Route A or Route B, and the Route A profile |
| Junctions and ports | The 10 nH of the junction above |
| Materials and films | Permittivities, and the thickness, permittivity and loss tangent of each Surface-EPR film |

### The route {#choose-the-geometric-approximation}

Whether the metal is a block of its real thickness (Route B) or a sheet of zero
thickness (Route A) is a model choice; a route is not a remedy for a mesh that
fails. [Route A and Route B](routes.qmd) explains both with the same pad.

::: {.callout-note title="Keep model and numerical comparisons separate"}
Refining a mesh studies one model's numerics. Changing the box, a material, a
port or the route studies a different model. Label the two kinds of study
separately, and keep units and mode or conductor identities when you compare
results.
:::

A source preview shows the geometry you declared, a mesh shows what the solver
will compute on, and only a solved field gives physical numbers. Energy that
was not computed, such as a film you did not request, stays missing; a loss
tangent you did not give stays unknown. Continue with
[Energy participation and Surface EPR](surface-epr.qmd) or
[Convergence and reports](../guides/convergence-and-reports.qmd).
